_readme: Settings for working ON THE HARNESS ITSELF — not the policy a scaffolded app gets, and not this project's security posture.

A scaffolded app is governed by template/base/.claude/settings.json plus the PreToolUse guard hooks (the pure-data rule table in .claude/hooks/lib/guard-rules.mjs). Those hooks are the deterministic layer; a permissions file is convenience, and it is not installed here because this repo is the harness, not a consumer of it.
So this file is deliberately permissive: routine work on the machinery never prompts. Only truly irreversible or outward-destructive actions sit in ask/deny.

Scratch-tree cleanup: the PERMISSIONS below leave /private/tmp prompt-free, but the bash-guard shim is stricter and denies the recursive-force delete in every flag spelling, anywhere — the guard is the deterministic layer and it does not read this file. Use `rm -r <dir>` for scratch trees. A maintainer meeting that rule is the point of the dogfood.

The guard is a TRIPWIRE, not a parser: it matches command TEXT, so a command whose payload merely quotes a denied spelling is denied too. That is a false positive in the safe direction, and it is why this note does not spell the pattern out.
FORKING THIS TEMPLATE: review this file before your first agent turn — you inherit it, and you may want a tighter default than the one the upstream maintainer runs.

DOGFOOD (0.2.0): the hooks below now run ON this repo. pretool-bash-guard is a three-line RE-EXPORT of the shipped guard — never a fork, so this repo is a live test of the exact bytes consumers get. pretool-write-guard cannot be shimmed (its subject is paths, and a consumer's tools/ is this repo's template/base/tools/), so it reuses the shipped hookio plumbing with a factory path table. stop-factory-gate runs the closure checks that nobody remembers to run — the pure-node machinery gates (hygiene, canary coverage, rule integrity, claims, floor lockstep, and the rest; STEPS in the hook is the authoritative list) plus the toolchain steps (eslint, tsc, knip, biome, and the tests/gates + tests/hooks red-proof corpus). Budget ~45-60 seconds, dominated by the tests step: the hook's own MEASURED note records ~46s total on the 16-core reference machine, ~31s of it the tests, against the 300s Stop budget below.

IT WILL BLOCK MAINTENANCE TURNS. That is the feature. A blocked maintainer turn means a consumer would have been blocked too, so a bug in the shipped guard surfaces on the machine of the person who can fix it. HARNESS_ALLOW_SELF_EDIT=1 is the human-in-the-loop escape, exactly as it is for consumers.

0.3.0 POSTURE PARITY. Until this release the factory allowed bare `Bash` with `acceptEdits`, set no `disableBypassPermissionsMode`, wired no PostToolUse hooks, and its write-guard omitted `installer/**` (only installer/lib/) and `template/migrations.json`. Every one of those is a posture the harness DEMANDS of a consumer and did not hold itself — and the maintainer's machine is where a bug in that posture is cheapest to find. The permission list stays deliberately broad for routine machinery work; what closed is the set of things the harness tells consumers are never routine.

POSTURE PARITY IS NOT POSTURE COPYING, and the .claude/hooks deny is where the two differ. The SHIPPED settings deny Edit/Write on .claude/hooks/** and .claude/settings.json at layer 1 (the permission model), which is right for a consumer: they never author hooks, the harness ships them. This repo DOES author them — they are the product — and layer 1 has no HARNESS_ALLOW_SELF_EDIT escape, so copying that deny here would make the factory unable to do its job while teaching maintainers to reach for bypassPermissions, the worst habit a guard can teach. The factory's control for those files is layer 2: pretool-write-guard's PROTECTED table covers all of `.claude/`, WITH the deliberate human-in-the-loop escape. Same property, the layer that has a door.

READ-ONLY TOOLS NEVER PROMPT. Read, Grep and Glob are allowed everywhere, including absolute paths outside the checkout (scratch scaffolds, worktrees), because they change nothing; the deny list above still keeps env files, keys and ~/.ssh out of reach. Cloud sessions honour this file too, so the rule saves the same prompts there.

CLOUD SESSIONS START READY. SessionStart runs .claude/hooks/session-start-cloud.sh, which does nothing unless CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE is true. In a cloud session it fetches full history and tags and installs the workspace, because each cloud session starts from a fresh clone and the Stop gate above needs both: its complexity step runs eslint from node_modules, and seeded-migrations fails on a shallow clone with no release tag. It always exits 0 and checks nothing.

AUTO MODE KEEPS ONLY NARROW RULES. Cloud project threads run in auto mode when their model supports it, and auto mode suspends the bare `Bash` allow above (a tool-wide rule grants arbitrary code execution), so every command no surviving rule matches goes to the classifier. The `Bash(...)` entries are the frozen-lockfile install, the checks CONTRIBUTING.md's "Local development" list says CI blocks on, and the scaffold render that starts its smoke test, each written as one exact invocation so auto mode keeps it and it runs without a classifier round-trip; outside auto mode the bare `Bash` already covers them, so they change nothing there. A `*` anywhere in a rule is a wildcard, which is why the suite is listed as `pnpm test` and not as its quoted `tests/**` glob: that rule would match any arguments in between. An exact rule still runs whatever the named script or test file contains, so an edit under tests/ or scripts/ followed by one of these commands is not reviewed; the docs accept that trade for rules like `Bash(npm test)`. Nothing here allows a wildcard over an interpreter or a package runner (`node *`, `pnpm exec *`), names a scaffold script that does not exist at this root (`pnpm lint`, `node tools/validate.mjs`), where a write could plant one, or lists a git or gh write, because the classifier is what catches the forms the deny list and the guard cannot spell (a `+refspec` push, a checkout that discards work) and an allow rule would skip it.

SUDO IS DENIED, NOT ASKED. An ask rule prompts even in auto mode, so a cloud thread that reached for `sudo` (to start dockerd) sat parked until someone answered the prompt. Cloud sessions run as root and never need it; as a deny it is refused at once, the agent retries without it, and nobody waits. A maintainer who needs root on their own machine runs that command themselves.
